NEUROMUSCULAR CASE REVIEW
Clinical Approach to a Patient Presenting
With Muscle Stiffness
Shameela N. Ahmed, MD, Tulio E. Bertorini, MD, Pushpa Narayanaswami, MD, and
Kandasami Senthilkumar, MD
Educational Objectives:
1. To learn to evaluate a patient presenting with muscle
stiffness.
2. To be familiar with the clinical features that differ-
entiate the various disorders presenting with muscle
stiffness.
3. To understand the diagnostic work-up of these patients.
4. To correlate the electrophysiological findings in each
condition with this clinical presentation.
Case Presentation
A 41-year-old right-handed African-American woman pre-
sented with gradual onset of stiffness and painful spasms
affecting her right lower extremity. The stiffness was per-
sistent and progressive. The spasms were precipitated by
sudden noise, anxiety, or fear. Her gait was impaired as a
result of the stiffness and spasms and she subsequently
suffered from falls. After several weeks she developed simi-
lar symptoms in the left lower extremity and her axial
musculature, with significant stiffness of her lower back.
She had to give up driving as a result of her symptoms and
was unable to continue her job, which involved standing
for long hours at a time. There were no other neurologic
symptoms. No other significant personal or family medical
history was obtained.
On examination the patient had no abnormalities of
higher mental functions, speech, or cranial nerves. Motor
examination revealed normal strength in all extremities
without wasting, myotonia, myokymia, or fasciculations.
Abdominal, and particularly lumbar paraspinal, muscles
were prominent and hard with stone-like consistency on
palpation. Muscle stretch reflexes were normal and plantar
responses were flexor. Sensory and cerebellar examinations
were normal. The general physical examination was nor-
mal except for exaggerated lordosis of lumbar spine and
stone-like consistency of lumbar paraspinal muscles on pal-
pation (Fig. 1).
What Is the Differential
Diagnosis of Muscle Stiffness?
The differential diagnosis of the patients presenting with
muscle stiffness is extensive; Table 1 outlines the diseases
that manifest these symptoms. The clinical examination is
crucial in narrowing down the diagnostic possibilities. The
following is a discussion of the various diseases that can
cause generalized muscle stiffness.
Akinetic-Rigid Syndromes
These are extrapyramidal, neurodegenerative disorders pre-
senting with muscular rigidity. The diagnosis is generally
made with the associated specific abnormalities in each
condition. The resting pill-rolling tremor, bradykinesia
and impaired postural reflexes of Parkinson’s disease,
1
impairment of extraocular movements in progressive su-
pranuclear palsy,
2 autonomic instability in Shy-Drager
syndrome, the pyramidal and cerebellar signs of olivopon-
tocerebellar atrophy, combined pyramidal and extrapyra-
midal signs, postural-action tremor and alien hand sign
seen in corticobasal degeneration,
3,4 and the dementia and
psychosis of diffuse Lewy body disease are very character-
istic. The case discussed here has none of these associated
characteristic clinical findings.
Stiff-Person Syndrome (SPS)
This is a syndrome characterized by co-contraction of ago-
nist and antagonist muscles, with resultant persistent stiff-
ness and muscle pain. There are superimposed painful
stimulus-induced spasms. The disease is usually slowly pro-

gressive with a primary involvement of the axial muscula-
ture but the extremities can also become affected. As a
result of the muscular stiffness and painful spasms, there
may be progressive impairment of gait and of daily activi-
ties resulting in severe incapacitation.
5
Antibodies against the enzyme glutamic acid decarbox-
ylase (GAD) have been found in 60% of SPS patients’ sera
and may be involved in pathogenesis.6 GAD is an enzyme

involved in the synthesis of the inhibitory neurotransmitter
gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA). GAD is also a major
auto-antigen of pancreatic islet beta-cells. Antibodies di-
rected against the pancreatic islet cells are also detected in
the sera of patients with stiff-person syndrome, and GAD
is the primary islet cell antigen they recognize.
7 Antibodies
against amphiphysin, a synaptic vesicle-associated protein,
can be elevated in patients with SPSand breast cancer. 8
Our patient has many of the characteristics of SPS. Elec-
tromyography (EMG) is important to differentiate this
condition from other disorders with similar presentations.
In SPS the EMG shows spontaneously firing motor units
in the affected muscles during attempts at relaxation and in
the absence of volitional contraction.
Progressive Encephalomyelitis
With Rigidity
This disease can present clinically with sensory and/or mo-
tor symptoms. There can be dysesthesias, hypoalgesia,
muscular rigidity, and stimulus-provoked spasms. Cranial
nerve involvement is prominent with nystagmus, ophthal-

moplegia, dysarthria, dysphagia, and deafness. The onset
is usually subacute (over a few weeks to months) even-
tually resulting in severe disability and death usually with-
in a 3- to 4-year period.
9 The pathology consists of an
interneuronitis of brainstem and spinal cord with subse-
quent release of the alpha motor neurons from the inhi-
bitory influence of the interneurons, resulting in their
uninhibited firing.
10 There is perivascular lymphocytic
infiltration and widespread degeneration of the long
tracts and the motor neurons in the lower brainstem
and the spinal cord resulting in the motor and sensory
signs.
The patient presented here did not have any mental
status changes, cranial nerve or sensory signs that may be
present in progressive encephalomyelitis. Hence, this was
an unlikely diagnosis in her case.
Dystonia
Dystonia is a disorder characterized by abnormal posture
produced by co-contraction of agonist and antagonist
muscles. Dystonias can be generalized or focal. The gen-
eralized dystonias are usually inherited, predominantly af-
fect the axial musculature, and improve with relaxation and
lying supine.
11 Focal dystonias affect a particular group of
muscles (for example, blepharospasm and torticollis), can
be associated with a tremor, and can be task-specific, for
example, writer’s cramp. Dystonia can also be associated
with other neurodegenerative disorders, in which case
other neurologic signs and symptoms are present. It can
also be a side effect of medications. Our patient had no task
specificity to her spasms and they did not subside with rest
or relaxation. There was no family history of similar mus-
cular spasms.
Tetanus
Tetanus is caused by the toxin of Clostridium tetani, which
is an anaerobic, spore-bearing bacillus present as a soil
contaminant. Usually there is a history of injury or surgery
in tetanus patients. On infection of wounds, the bacteria
release the toxin by autolysis and the latter spreads to the
central nervous system by retrograde axonal transport. The
tetanus toxin prevents release of the inhibitory neurotrans-
mitters GABA and glycine by cleavage of synaptobrevin, a
protein in the synaptic vesicles, hence producing unre-
strained reflex activity of skeletal muscles and the auto-
nomic system. Clinically the patient can have rapidly pro-
gressive, localized, or generalized rigidity of muscles with
superimposed spontaneous and stimulus-sensitive spasms.
Trismus is very pathognomonic. Dyspnea, asphyxia, and
cyanosis can occur as a result of involvement of respiratory
muscles.
11
In the presented case, the onset of the muscular stiffness
was insidious and not temporarily related to any injury.
There was no involvement of the jaw musculature or re-
spiratory distress to indicate the possibility of tetanus.
Myelopathy
Structural lesions involving the central spinal cord can pro-
duce pain, stiffness, stimulus-induced spasms, and abnor-
mal limb postures. The etiologies include multiple sclero-
sis, syringomyelia, hydromyelia, tumor, trauma, and my-
elitis. The pathogenesis of the spasticity and spasms is
considered to be disruption of the inhibitory interneuronal
circuits with resultant continuous motor unit discharge of
the spinal alpha motor neurons. Clinically in cervical le-
sions, the patients have segmental weakness and wasting,
hypo- or areflexia in upper extremities, hyperreflexia and
spasticity in lower extremities with positive Babinski signs

as well as segmental and tract sensory signs.
Myelopathy is an unlikely diagnosis in the presented case
because of the lack of sensory level, hyperreflexia, Babinski
signs, or spasticity.
Neuromyotonia
Neuromyotonia or Isaac’s syndrome is a condition charac-
terized by myokymia, stiffness, and impaired relaxation
(wave-like contractions of muscles).
12,13 It affects both
children and adults. The onset of the disease is gradual.
Patients experience muscle aches and cramps. The distal,
proximal, and cranial muscles are affected. Stiffness and
myokymia are present at rest and increase on attempts at
contraction, thereby limiting mobility. Gait is impaired.
Abnormal and persistent posturing of hands and feet can
be seen. Muscle stretch reflexes are usually depressed.
Stimulus-sensitive myoclonus is absent, and percussion
myotonia occurs infrequently. Patients can also have auto-
nomic manifestation such as hyperhydrosis and tachycar-
dia. The continuous muscle activity is abolished by curare
but persists during sleep, general and local anesthesia.
Neuromyotonia is usually an autoimmune disorder
5,14
caused by antibodies directed against voltage-gated potas-
sium channels in the peripheral nerves producing nerve
hyperexcitability and persistent abnormal motor unit ac-
tivity. An inherited form has been described with the gene
abnormality on chromosome 12.
15 Other associations in-
clude episodic ataxia and encephalopathy (Morvan’s syn-
drome). Myasthenia gravis, thymoma, systemic sclerosis,
and neuropathies (including motor neuron disease, heredi-
tary and demyelinating peripheral neuropathies) also oc-
cur. Paraneoplastic neuromyotonia has been reported in
association with small cell carcinoma of the lung.
16 Elec-
tromyographic studies are necessary to confirm or rule out
the diagnosis.
Although some clinical features of neuromyotonia are
present in this case, there was no evidence of myokymia or
autonomic involvement. Her spasms disappeared during
sleep.

Tetany
Tetany is a sustained, abnormal posture assumed by muscle
groups. There is increased axonal excitability secondary to
sustained membrane depolarization and lowered action po-
tential threshold. Spontaneous discharges, between 5 and
15 Hz in frequency, arise in the peripheral axons. Low
extracellular calcium level leads to unopposed sodium ex-
citation of the axonal membrane. Ischemia and alkalosis
secondary to hyperventilation can perpetuate the condi-
tion. Tetany is usually caused by hypocalcemia (as seen in
hypoparathyroidism and severe respiratory alkalosis), but it
can occur with hypomagnesemia. An idiopathic normocal-
cemic tetany (hereditary and acquired form) have been
described.
17,18 There is a predilection for laryngeal muscles
and distal limb muscles to be affected.
Clinically tetany can be elicited by tapping on the facial
nerve at the stylomastoid foramen (Chvostek ’s sign) or
with the ischemic forearm test (Trousseau’s sign). Treatment
is with calcium, magnesium, and membrane-stabilizing
agents such as phenytoin. Tocainide, a lidocaine analog, has
also proven to be of benefit in treating the painful spasms of
tetany.
19
There were no clinical findings of tetany in the patient
presented here. She did not have Chvostek ’s sign, her
spasms were predominantly axial and proximal rather than
appendicular and distal as occurs in tetany.
Benign Cramps
The entity of benign cramps deserves mention here. A
typical cramp can be defined as an involuntary, irregular,
intermittent, painful, usually brief, and focal skeletal
muscle contraction during which spontaneously firing
muscle action potentials are recorded on EMG ( “cramp
potentials”).
20 Benign, painful cramps, accompanied by
stiffness of affected muscles, can be seen in otherwise
healthy people, or they can be associated with dehydration,
electrolyte disturbances, pregnancy, motor neuron disease,
hypothyroidism, and polyneuropathies. They occur during
rest or sleep and can be provoked by or follow strenuous
exercise. The painful spasm cannot be voluntarily relaxed.
Stretching the muscle usually overcomes the spasm. Exces-
sive excitability and spontaneous firing of the motor nerve
endings is the presumed abnormality. Cramps vary in pre-
sentation and are usually aggravated by exercise. This was
not the presentation in our case.
Hypothyroid Myopathy
Hypothyroidism is characterized by myalgias, muscle stiff-
ness, and spasms. Clinically, delayed contraction and re-
laxation of muscle stretch reflexes, percussion myoedema,
and occasionally myokymia can be demonstrated. The
pathogenesis of delayed contraction is said to be decreased
myosin-ATPase, and the delayed relaxation is caused by
decreased rate of release and re-accumulation of calcium in
the endoplasmic reticulum.
21 Other neurologic complica-
tions, such as neuropathy and psychomotor retardation,
can be present in addition to systemic symptoms, all of
which are absent in the presented case, making hypothy-
roidism an unlikely diagnosis.
Myotonic Syndromes
The myotonic syndromes are hereditary conditions, char-
acterized by myotonia. Myotonia is a sustained contraction
of the muscle following a voluntary, mechanical, or elec-
trical stimulation and is the result of prolonged excitation
of the muscle membrane. Myotonic syndromes are briefly
discussed here.
Myotonia may be the first clinical feature of myotonic
dystrophy and may precede dystrophic features by several
years. Myotonic dystrophy (DM1) is an autosomal-

dominant disorder (chromosome 19q13.3) with a high
degree of penetrance. The mutation responsible for DM is
the unstable expansion of a trinucleotide repeat, (CTG)n,
in the 3’-untranslated region of the myotonin-protein ki-
nase gene.
22 It affects not only smooth and skeletal muscle,
but also endocrine glands, ocular lens, skin, and cerebrum.
The masseters, facial, forearm, hand, and pretibial muscles
are particularly affected. Involvement of heart, esophagus,
uterine muscle, testicles, and lens of the eye by the dystro-
phic process has been well described. There is a group of
patients with myotonic dystrophy in which the genetic
defect is not located on chromosome 19 (DM2).
Proximal myotonic myopathy (PROMM) is a clinical
variant of myotonic dystrophy.
23 Most families have been
linked to a locus on chromosome 3q21.24 There is muscle
weakness affecting mainly proximal and axial muscles.
Early cataracts can be a feature but facial muscles are less
involved. Clinical myotonia is less prominent than in myo-
tonic dystrophy.
PROMM and myotonic dystrophy type 2 (DM2) may
be allelic disorders. As discussed, myotonic dystrophy type
2 lacks the CTG repeat expansion on chromosome 19q.
Recent reports suggest that DM2 is caused by a CCTG
(tetranucleotide)-expansion located in intron 1 of the zinc
finger protein 9 (ZNF9) gene.
25
Myotonia congenita is a nonprogressive disease mani-
fested clinically as muscle stiffness and spasms that are
induced by voluntary movements, especially after rest. The
spasms tend to abate with continued exercise. The condi-
tion can be inherited as an autosomal-dominant (Thom-
sen’s disease) or autosomal-recessive (Becker’s generalized
myotonia) trait. It is associated with abnormalities linked
to a gene (CLCN 1) on chromosome 7q35 encoding the
skeletal muscle chloride channel.
26 An unusual form of
painful myotonia congenita associated with a mutation in
the skeletal muscle voltage-gated sodium channel
alpha-subunit gene has also been described.
27 The diagno-
sis is established by the presence of clinical and electrical

myotonia. The family history and muscular hypertrophy

Paramyotonia congenita (Von Eulenberg’s disease) is an
autosomal-dominant sodium channelopathy. It is caused
by point mutations in the gene encoding the alpha-subunit
of the skeletal muscle sodium channel (SCN4A). Patients
experience attacks of myotonia and periodic paralysis. The
symptoms are induced by cold and aggravated by exercise,
hence the name paramyotonia.
28 During attacks, serum
potassium is elevated or high-normal and the serum so-
dium is low.
Schwartz-Jampel syndrome is a osteochondromuscular
dystrophy that was first described by Schwartz and Jam-
pel.
29 The disease has an autosomal-recessive inheritance
and is seen as a childhood and a rare neonatal form. 30
Clinical features include bone abnormalities, dwarfism, fa-
cial and ocular anomalies, gait abnormalities resulting from
stiffness, and severe voluntary and percussion myotonia.
Intelligence is preserved. Mutations in the perlecan gene
(HSPG2) have been reported to cause Schwartz-Jampel
syndrome. Perlecan, a large heparan sulfate proteoglycan, is
a component of the basement membrane, and it has been
suggested that it has an important role in neuromuscular
function and cartilage formation.
31
Myotonia was not mechanically or electrically elicited in
our patient. The history and clinical examination of our
case were not consistent with any of the aforementioned
disorders.
Metabolic Myopathies
Metabolic myopathies can present with myalgias, and
exercise-induced contractures and myoglobinuria. A con-
tracture is an involuntary muscle shortening that is electri-
cally silent. The duration is generally seconds to minutes
but can last up to hours. In contrast to cramps, contrac-
tures cannot be relieved by massaging or stretching the
affected muscle. Included in this category are several dis-
orders of glycogen metabolism, such as myophosphorylase
deficiency (type V glycogenosis, McArdle’s disease), phos-
phofructokinase deficiency (type VII glycogenosis, Tarui’s
disease), phosphorylaseb kinase deficiency (type VIII gly-
cogenosis), phosphoglycerate kinase deficiency (type IX
glycogenosis), muscle phosphoglycerate mutase deficiency
(type X glycogenosis), and lactate dehydrogenase deficiency
(type XI glycogenosis).
32
Our patient suffered from progressive stiffness and ri-
gidity of muscles as opposed to predominantly
exercise-induced cramps as seen in metabolic myopathies.
She did not give a history of myoglobinuria.
Brody’s Disease
Brody’s disease is characterized by impaired muscle relax-
ation, particularly during exercise.33 A deficiency of a cal-
cium transport protein in the sarcoplasmic reticulum of
type 2 fibers may be the etiology of the impaired relax-
ation.
34 In skeletal muscle and cultured muscle cells of
patients with Brody’s disease, the activity of sarcoplasmic
reticulum calcium-ATPase is reduced by approximately
50%, although the total concentration remains normal,
indicating possibly a structural modification. Diseased
muscle shows a delayed restoration of Ca++ after stimula-
tion.
35 The disorder has X-linked inheritance. Symptoms
are generally evident in the first decade.
As a result of the age and sex, the clinical picture and the
lack of exercised-induced stiffness make this an unlikely
diagnosis in our case.
Rippling Muscle Disease
This syndrome has been described in a hereditary36–38 and
sporadic form. The hereditary form is mapped to chromo-

some 1q41 and is autosomal dominant. The sporadic form
has its onset in the 30- to 55-year age group and can be
associated with thymoma and myasthenia gravis.
39 Clinical
features include muscle cramps, pain involving the legs
more than the arms, which are exacerbated by exercise, and
stiffness. A wave-like ripple evoked by stretch or percussion
moves over the muscle for approximately 5 to 20 seconds,
during which the muscle is electrically silent. Immunosup-
pressants can help the sporadic form. Dantrolene has been
tried in the hereditary form.
The lack of the characteristic “rippling phenomenon”
makes the diagnosis unlikely in our patient.
Myopathies With Muscle Fibrosis
Although unlikely in this patient, stiffness of the muscles
can also be the result of muscle fibrosis as seen particularly
in Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy, but also in Beth-
lem myopathy and some limb-girdle muscular dystrophies.
Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy is an X-linked re-
cessive disease. Cases with autosomal-dominant inheri-
tance have been described
40 with genetic mutations in the
lamin A/C gene 1q21.2-q21.3.41 Muscular weakness, car-
diac involvement, and contractures that initially involve the
flexor muscles of knee and elbow joints are cardinal features.
The disease can manifest in childhood, the progression can be
slow, and the patients might become wheelchair bound in the
second or third decade of life. EMG shows brief motor unit
potentials and occasionally fibrillations.
Our patient presented without weakness and with rigidity
instead of contractures with no evidence of cardiomyopathy.
Drug-Induced Muscle Stiffness
Increased muscle tone has been described during etretinate
therapy.
42 Peripheral nerve block extinguished the in-
creased muscle tone indicating that this is caused by in-
creased peripheral nerve excitability. Intramuscular injec-
tions of drugs such as pentazocine for pain relief can induce
muscle fibrosis and stiffness.
43

The patient presented here did not receive medications.
There was no muscle fibrosis.
What Is the Diagnostic Workup
of Patients With Muscle Stiffness?
As discussed, the clinical examination is of foremost im-
portance in the diagnosis of a patient presenting with
muscle stiffness. The algorithm outlined inFigure. 2 can
help the clinician in the localization.
The evaluation of patients presenting with muscle stiff-
ness should include a complete blood count, a complete
metabolic profile, including Ca
+2 and Mg+2, thyroid func-
tion tests, measurement of creatine kinase levels, and nerve
conduction studies. Determination of F/M and H/M ra-
tios as well as testing of the masseter inhibitory reflex and
silent period could also be useful. Needle EMG is most
valuable.
Additional studies that are necessary based on the clinical
findings and abnormalities on initial tests are outlined in
Table 2.
Electrodiagnostic Studies in
Patients With Muscle Stiffness
Stiff-person Syndrome
Nerve conduction studies are usually normal. Motor neu-
ron hyperexcitability has been documented by high
H-reflex to M-wave amplitude ratios (normal<0.7 for calf
H reflexes) and there is a high F-wave to M-wave ampli-
tude ratio,
44 although this has not been found by others.45
During EMG, continuous motor unit potentials indistin-
guishable from voluntary activity are seen during attempts
at relaxation. After voluntary contraction this activity is
present concurrently in agonist and antagonist muscles,
and is maximally seen in the axial muscles. There are rhyth-
mic, synchronous motor unit bursts of 50 to 60 millisec-
onds duration and 5 to 6 Hz frequency. The bursts may be
interrupted by spasms of rapid activity and full interference
pattern lasting more than 4 seconds. The spasms and spon-
taneous discharges disappear during sleep, administration
of diazepam, general and spinal anesthesia, following pro-
caine block of the peripheral nerve, and after infusion of
curare. There is no evidence of myokymic or neuromyo-
tonic discharges.
The silent period
46 and masseter inhibitory reflex47 are
normal whereas the exteroceptive reflexes45 and the startler
response are exaggerated.48 Recently Sandbrink et al., 49
using transcranial magnetic stimulation with paired
stimuli, found an increased facilitation of the limb motor
evoked responses.
Dystonia
Electromyographic finding characteristic of a dystonia is
the evidence of focal continuous motor unit activity in
co-contracting agonist and antagonist muscles relieved by
curare and diazepam. The differentiation from stiff-person
syndrome is clinical.
5

Tetanus
There is spontaneous firing of motor units that decreases
with diazepam and neuromuscular blocks. There is a loss of
the masseteric silent period as well as the silent period that
is seen normally after stimulation of peripheral nerves. This
silent period is indicative of reflex inhibition of motor neu-
rons by the inhibitory interneurons, which are affected in
tetanus.
47
Neuromyotonia
In neuromyotonia, electromyography reveals continuous
muscle fiber activity that persists during sleep, administra-
tion of diazepam, and general or spinal anesthesia, but
disappears with local neuromuscular blockade with curare.
Doublet, triplet, or multiplet single-unit discharges with a
high interburst frequency are seen. Fasciculations and fi-
brillations can also be seen.
12,13
Hypothyroidism
In this condition the EMG can be entirely normal or can
reveal small motor units with early recruitment on volun-
tary contractions. Bizarre high-frequency discharges can be
seen, but myotonia is not present.
Muscle Cramps
EMG shows runs of motor unit activity during the
pre-cramp phase and high-frequency, high-voltage motor
unit discharges during the cramp. Stretching the muscle
usually overcomes the cramp (“cramp potential”).
Tetany
EMG shows grouped motor unit discharges firing asyn-
chronously at 4 to 5 Hz (doublets, triplets, multiplets) with
periods of relative silence in between them. Maximal in-
terference pattern is seen during the spasm of tetany.
5,17
Myotonic Syndromes
Needle EMG shows myotonic discharges with the charac-
teristic “dive bomber sound” consist of trains of potentials
that wax and wane in frequency and amplitude. Motor
unit potentials may be low amplitude, short duration, and
polyphasic. In paramyotonia congenita, myotonic dis-
charges are lessened by cold, despite increasing stiffness of
muscles. The myotonic discharges do not decrease with
administration of curare or diazepam. The compound
muscle action potential amplitude can decrease with re-
petitive nerve stimulation. In Schwartz-Jampel syndrome,
EMG shows continuous motor unit activity similar to that
seen in neuromyotonia, with high-frequency complex re-
petitive discharges as well as myotonic discharges.
29
Metabolic Myopathies
During the contractures, the muscles are electrically silent
on EMG and are thus distinguished from the involuntary
muscle spasms of other diseases.
5
Diagnostic Studies in Our Patient
The main disorders that would be considered in the differ-
ential diagnosis of the presented case include SPS, chronic
tetany, neuromyotonia, and the myotonic disorders.
Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel,
and liver function tests were normal. Serum creatine ki-
nase, vitamin B12/folate levels, thyroid function tests, hu-
man immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibody, rapid

This was unaffected by the patient’s attempts at relaxation
and subsided with the administration of diazepam intrave-
nously. There were no doublets or triplets, myotonic or
complex repetitive discharges, and the motor units were
normal in configuration. The silent period s during stimu-
lation of the median nerve at the wrist and the masseter
inhibitory reflex were normal.
Islet cell cytoplasmic antibody (ICAP) titers were el-
evated in the serum (1:61,400; normal, <1:120). Amphi-
physin and GAD antibodies were not assayed.
What Is the Diagnosis in the
Presented Case?
Our patient had slowly progressive muscle stiffness with
superimposed stimulus-induced muscle spasms. The per-
tinent clinical finding was the rock-like hardness of ab-
dominal and paraspinal muscles on palpation, and exag-
gerated lumbar lordosis.
Serum islet-cell cytoplasmic antibodies were elevated.
EMG revealed continuous motor unit activity in the ab-
sence of volitional contraction of muscles. The administra-
tion of diazepam abolished this activity. There was no
myokymia or myotonia.
Thus, the history, clinical presentation, laboratory, and
EMG findings were consistent with a diagnosis of SPS.
What Is Stiff-person Syndrome?
Described first by Moersch and Woltman50 in 1956, who
termed it stiff-man syndrome, it is now better termed
stiff-person syndrome as a result of its occurrence in both
sexes. The onset is in the fourth and fifth decades, with the
mean age of onset being 41.2 years.
51 The clinical index of
suspicion is generally low, and in one case report the me-
dian interval between onset of symptoms and diagnosis was
up to 18 years, mean duration being 6.2 years. The com-
mon symptoms are summarized in Table 3.
5,51–53 These
include progressive, generalized muscle stiffness, promi-
nent lordosis, painful spasms, and difficulty ambulating.
Dalakas et al.
53 suggested the following criteria for the
diagnosis of SPS: 1) insidious onset of muscular rigidity in
the limbs and axial muscles, most prominent in the ab-
dominal and thoracolumbar paraspinals, with difficulty in
turning or bending; 2) continuous co-contraction of ago-
nist and antagonist muscles with inability to relax, as con-
firmed clinically and electrophysiologically; 3) episodic
spasms superimposed on the rigidity and precipitated by
unexpected noises, tactile stimuli, or emotional upset; and
4) absence of any other neurologic disease or chronic pain
syndromes that can explain stiffness and rigidity.
Variants of Stiff-person Syndrome
The “stiff-limb syndrome” described by Baker et al. 54 is
considered to be a variant of the stiff-person syndrome.
The symptoms include progressive stiffness that begins in
one limb and spreads to involve other muscles. Abnormal,
fixed posturing of the affected limb is characteristic.
55 The
truncal musculature, brainstem, and sphincters may be in-
volved in later stages, along with pronounced lordosis and
deformities of the spine. An association with malignancy
has been observed.
56
SPS has been described as a paraneoplastic syndrome in
women with breast cancer. 57 These patients can have
anti-amphiphysin I antibodies in serum. Amphiphysin I is
a nerve terminal protein and plays a role in endocytosis.
58
These antibodies have also been described in other para-
neoplastic syndromes such as small cell cancer of the lung
and paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis,
58,59 and hence are
not specific for any one paraneoplastic syndrome. Their

presence in a patient with SPS should prompt the physi-
cian to look for malignancy, although amphiphysin anti-
bodies have been reported in atypical cases of SPS without
associated malignancy.
60
Frequently SPS can be associated with other autoim-
mune diseases, most commonly insulin-dependent diabe-
tes mellitus (IDDM). Both diseases share a major
auto-antigen, the enzyme glutamic acid decarboxylase
(GAD).
61,62 GAD is located in the beta cells of the pan-

creas and in the GABA-producing neurons of the periph-
eral and central nervous system. Antibodies directed
against the islet-cell antigen GAD are found in over 80%
of the patients with IDDM. These are called the islet-cell
cytoplasmic antibodies (ICAP). Hashimoto’s thyroiditis,
pernicious anemia, celiac disease, and seizures have been
described in SPS patients. SPS associated with thymoma
and subsequent myasthenia gravis has also been described,
with improvement of symptoms after thymectomy.
44 Sei-
zures occur in approximately 25% of patients with SPS,53
and might be related to increased cortical excitability and
decreased inhibitory neurotransmitter, GABA.
Anti-GAD antibodies have been identified in the CSF
and sera of 60% of the patients with SPS.
62,63 These are
directed against the GABAergic neurons and specifically
against glutamic acid decarboxylase, which is an enzyme
involved in the synthesis of GABA.
The progressive muscular stiffness and rigidity clinically
seen in SPS is presumably caused by an imbalance between
the excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters involved in
control of muscle tone.
63 The major inhibitory neurotrans-
mitter in the central motor pathways is gamma aminobu-
tyric acid (GABA).
In a study of 18 patients with SPS, markedly high in-
trathecal antibody response against neuronal GAD-65 epi-
tope was identified, indicating a clonal B cell activation in
the CNS.
64 Furthermore, the anti GAD-65 antibodies in
the CSF and sera of these patients reacted strongly with
recombinant GAD-65, as opposed to controls.
64 Hence,
anti-GAD 65 antibodies, when confirmed with immuno-
blots, are highly specific for SPS. They can be pathogenic
by way of impairment of GABA synthesis, which brings
about uninhibited alpha motor neuronal firing and in-
creased tone and muscle stiffness.
What Is the Treatment for SPS?
Symptomatic treatment with high doses of diazepam, clo-
nazepam, and baclofen has been the mainstay of treatment;
however, sedation has been the major cumbersome side
effect. Oral and intra-thecal baclofen have been helpful,
and clinical and electromyographic improvement have
been noted.
64 It is important to mention that abrupt with-
drawal of intrathecal baclofen has been associated with
sudden deaths.
65
Immunomodulation with plasma exchange and intrave-
nous immunoglobulin (IVIG) have been found to be ef-
fective in reducing the symptoms of stiffness and
spasms.
66–68 A study by Dalakas et al.69 found that IVIG
administration has a significant benefit over placebo in the
patients with SPS who were either not responding to ben-
zodiazepines, or were having significant side effects at
therapeutic doses. In some cases, immunosuppression with
azathioprine or corticosteroids has also been tried with
moderate success.
51
Sodium valproate has been used in the treatment of
SPS.69 Vigabatrin, which is a GABAergic anti-epileptic,
has decreased the stiffness and improved the ambulation in
some cases.
70 Tiagabine71 has been beneficial in reducing
the spasms.
Treatment of the malignancy in paraneoplastic cases of
SPS can help improve the symptoms. In cases of myasthenia
gravis and thymoma associated with SPS, improvement of
the stiffness has been documented after thymectomy.
44,52
Botulinum toxin A has been successfully used to treat
the spasms and rigidity of the SPS. Interestingly, it has
been reported that unilateral injection frequently produces
relief of spasms bilaterally,
72 possibly as a result of hema-

togenous spread of the toxin.
Clinical Course of the Presented
Case
The patient had a CT scan of her chest that revealed a
hypertrophic thymus. The thymus was removed surgically
without improvement in her symptoms. Acetylcholine re-
ceptor antibody titers were not elevated. She was subse-
quently treated with diazepam and baclofen with relief of
rigidity and spasms. She continues to have lumbar lordosis
and stiffness, but is ambulating without support and is
currently also on tizanidine which is helping control her
symptoms. When her symptoms worsen so as to interfere
with her activities of daily living, she receives IVIG treat-
ments that help control the spasms.
Summary
SPS is a disorder that needs to be considered and recog-
nized in patients presenting with muscle stiffness and
spasms, because early diagnosis and appropriate treatment
can substantially help the patient and prevent significant
injuries and limitations that occur with the natural pro-
gression of the disease. A diagnosis of SPS should prompt
investigation for thymoma and an occult malignancy, be-
cause SPS can be a paraneoplastic syndrome. SPS may be
associated with other autoimmune diseases such as IDDM
and Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, and a work-up for these dis-
orders is appropriate. Symptomatic treatment with benzo-
diazepines and other GABAergic medications is commonly
used and immunomodulating therapy, especially IVIG, is
beneficial.

segments.text:
Case Presentation
A 41-year-old right-handed African-American woman pre-
sented with gradual onset of stiffness and painful spasms
affecting her right lower extremity. The stiffness was per-
sistent and progressive. The spasms were precipitated by
sudden noise, anxiety, or fear. Her gait was impaired as a
result of the stiffness and spasms and she subsequently
suffered from falls. After several weeks she developed simi-
lar symptoms in the left lower extremity and her axial
musculature, with significant stiffness of her lower back.
She had to give up driving as a result of her symptoms and
was unable to continue her job, which involved standing
for long hours at a time. There were no other neurologic
symptoms. No other significant personal or family medical
history was obtained.
On examination the patient had no abnormalities of
higher mental functions, speech, or cranial nerves. Motor
examination revealed normal strength in all extremities
without wasting, myotonia, myokymia, or fasciculations.
Abdominal, and particularly lumbar paraspinal, muscles
were prominent and hard with stone-like consistency on
palpation. Muscle stretch reflexes were normal and plantar
responses were flexor. Sensory and cerebellar examinations
were normal. The general physical examination was nor-
mal except for exaggerated lordosis of lumbar spine and
stone-like consistency of lumbar paraspinal muscles on pal-
pation (Fig. 1).

tion of diazepam abolished this activity. There was no
myokymia or myotonia.
Thus, the history, clinical presentation, laboratory, and
EMG findings were consistent with a diagnosis of SPS.
